hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? have you ever changed so much you barely recognize who you used to be?
options: then today’s question is yours. listen.
I feel the same as ever
interesting. let’s look a little closer.

steps.line: A wandering seeker named Vacchagotta came to the Buddha with a big question. He sat down and asked it straight out.
“Master Gotama,” he said, “is there a self?” A real me, at the center of everything?

steps.q: The Buddha stays silent. What do you guess Vacchagotta does next?
o: Argues until he gets an answer
Asks it the other way round
steps.why: He flips it: “Then is there no self?” Silence again. Only then does he get up and leave.

steps.line: The Buddha was silent. “Then is there no self?” Again the Buddha was silent. So Vacchagotta got up and left.
His attendant Ananda was puzzled. “Why didn’t you answer him?”
“If I had said yes,” the Buddha explained, “he would have held on to a fixed self. That wouldn’t fit the truth that nothing can be held as a self.”

steps.q: And if he’d said, “No, there’s no self”? What would have gone wrong?
o: He’d think he once had a self and lost it
He’d think the Buddha didn’t know
He’d feel the Buddha was mocking him
steps.why: In the sutta the Buddha says a no would only deepen the confusion: “the self I had before is gone.” A loss, not a freedom.

steps.line: “And if I had said no, he was already confused. He would think, ‘I used to have a self, and now it’s gone.’”

steps.q: Vacchagotta asked other big questions too. Which one did the Buddha also leave unanswered?
o: Can anyone wake up, or only monks?
Is the world eternal, or not?
steps.why: Tradition lists questions he set aside: is the world eternal, is it infinite, what is a Buddha after death. Answering them, he said, wouldn’t help anyone end suffering.

steps.line: Today, say the word “I” and try to point to it. The body has changed. Moods turn twice before lunch. Who’s in there?
steps.label: today

say: the third mark is anatta, not-self. the buddha would go through what a person is made of, the body, feelings, perceptions, mental formations and consciousness, and ask of each: is it lasting? can you rest on it? is it me?
theravada teachers stress seeing those five heaps as not-self. mahayana teachers speak of emptiness, and some of a buddha-nature in every being. either way, the question stays open: look, and see.

steps.q: Try the Buddha’s test on this morning’s bad mood. Is it right to call it “my self”?
o: Yes: I felt it, so it’s part of me
No: it came and went, so it can’t be “me”
Only if I feel it every day
steps.why: In his second sermon the Buddha asks this of body, feelings, perceptions, formations and consciousness: whatever changes, is it fit to call “this is mine, this I am, this is my self”? The monks answer: no.

steps.q: The Buddha wouldn’t say yes or no. So what is not-self mainly asking you to do?
o: Believe firmly that you don’t exist
Look at each part of you and ask, “is this me?”
steps.why: Not a belief to hold, and not a ban on “I.” A way of looking: is this lasting? is this me? Silence left that looking to him.

today.say: today, three times, notice a thought or feeling arrive. before calling it “me,” just ask: did i choose this, or did it just arrive? don’t answer. keep looking.
options: I’d rather just think about it
that’s fine. the question will keep.

sources: Ananda Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 44.10): Vacchagotta asks “is there a self?” and “is there no self?”; the Buddha’s silence; his explanation to Ananda (siding with eternalists or annihilationists; not in line with “all things are not-self”; Vacchagotta, already confused, would think “the self I had before is now gone”)
Anattalakkhana Sutta (Samyutta Nikaya 22.59): the five aggregates questioned; “this is mine, this I am, this is my self”
Mahayana teaching on emptiness (e.g. the Heart Sutra) and buddha-nature (e.g. the Mahayana Mahaparinirvana Sutra, tathagatagarbha texts)
